podcast.body: Released in the fall of 1969, this powerful song served as an anti-Vietnam War anthem. It specifically targets the "fortunate sons," who were the offspring of the rich and powerful, capable of escaping the draft for military service. The song's core message highlighted the hypocrisy of supporting a war without having to bear its personal costs. "The message was, hey, it's easy to support the war if you never have to pay any of the costs for it."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.body: The song "Fortunate Son" was notably absent from the soundtrack of the TV show *Mad Men*. The series, aiming to capture the popular culture of the 1960s as it was actually lived, deliberately avoided what it considered cliched protest music of the era. "no fortune at sun by credence clear water revival."

srcs.source: Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia

podcast.body: This song had a very clear anti-Vietnam War stance, a theme that Bruce Springsteen would later pick up in his own music. "So if you listen to Fortune at Sun and it's got a very clear anti-Vietnam war stance, which is a theme that Bruce Springsteen would pick up."

podcast.body: This song, written by John Fogerty, was inspired by the disparity where children of wealthy and connected parents received draft deferments for the Vietnam War. It was controversially played during Donald Trump's presidential campaign, despite Trump himself receiving five draft deferments and at the same time being reported to have called soldiers and war dead "losers and suckers." "fortune at sun by credence clearwater revival, which was inspired by the kids of rich and connected parents getting draft affirmants for Vietnam, which is exactly what happened with Donald Trump five times."
